item.title: Autoimmunity and the Stories Women Tell About Illness
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

For many women, being good has always meant being useful. Their sense of worth becomes tied to anticipating everyone else’s needs, taking responsibility for problems that aren’t theirs, and making sure no one is disappointed. Their own needs fall to the bottom of the list. Over time, it can become difficult to remember what it feels like to put themselves first.

What are we afraid will happen if we stop being who others expect us to be?

Sara Hirsh Bordo spent 15 years as a documentary filmmaker telling women’s stories before she began examining her own. Her experiences with serious illness led her to question the rules she’d been living by, and the result is her first book, Autoimmunity and the Good Girls. She calls herself a “recovering good girl.”

When we spoke, she kept returning to one question: What are we afraid will happen if we stop being who others expect us to be?

The Fear Beneath the Shoulds

We all know the vocabulary. I should do more. I should be available. I should be able to manage all of it. Bordo thinks the shoulds are not where this starts.

“I don’t think the ‘shoulds’ come first. I think the fears come first,” Bordo says.

She describes the questions that can arise when we begin challenging expectations we’ve lived with for years: What will my family think? Will I disappoint someone? What happens if I become someone new—and what if I don’t like that person?

“I think that if you can survive incremental levels of disappointing other people, all of a sudden, there’s freedom that comes in the place of those pockets,” Bordo says.

For Bordo, recognizing those fears meant reconsidering the rules she’d built her life around. She began questioning the expectations she’d inherited and making room for new ways of thinking about herself and her relationships.

“I think that if you can survive incremental levels of disappointing other people, all of a sudden, there’s freedom that comes in the place of those pockets,” she says.

She also recognizes how deeply these fears can be passed down through generations. They’re not just her own, she explains, but part of the expectations she saw reflected in her mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother.

She said this the morning after a Zoom conversation with a book club of about 17 women of color, where the conversation about permission brought several of them to tears. The discussion prompted reflection on expectations and beliefs that some women had carried for decades.

The Stories We Inherit

Bordo’s question started with a pattern. The women around her who had been diagnosed with chronic or autoimmune conditions were all eldest or only daughters, herself included. At first, she assumed it was connected to birth order. So she and what she calls her “crack team of volunteers” started calling the CDC and the NIH. They found research about birth order and health in general, but nothing on autoimmune disease specifically.

She then conducted an informal survey of 300 women in the U.S. with autoimmune conditions, and 70 percent reported being eldest or only daughters.

She then conducted an informal survey of 300 women in the U.S. with autoimmune conditions, and 70 percent reported being eldest or only daughters. A few of the others wrote her personal notes describing how they’d taken on significant responsibility for others, despite not being the eldest or only daughter.

The survey was not a scientific study and had no comparison group, so the findings cannot establish a connection between birth order and autoimmune disease. But the notes stayed with her, because they pointed past birth order to something she describes as “heightened responsibility too soon.”

These observations also led Bordo to think differently about the relationship between personal experiences and physical health.

“Our body doesn’t just speak science, it speaks story,” Bordo says.

A doctor she names as Dr. Carmona then introduced her to epigenetics, the study of how changes in gene activity can occur without altering the underlying DNA sequence. She used it to map experiences from different chapters of her life against what her body might have been doing at the time. She is clear that this is her own framework and not a medical explanation. But it gave her a way to think about the body’s immune response in autoimmune disease, and about permission as the story we tell about who we’re allowed to be.

Permission, she told me, “is just the ground floor.”

To describe what it feels like when fear loosens, she reaches for a heist movie. She means it as a picture of how the change felt; she doesn’t claim it explains how autoimmune disease starts or ends.

“I feel like that level of fear and the power of fear is holding the space for freedom. And when freedom lives more than fear does, I think that’s when we are jackknifed into an immune system that actually starts almost unlocking itself. And then it’s like an Ocean’s Eleven scene. They’re opening the safe, and it’s like the inner workings of the safe, and the wheels are spinning, and then the doors are opening, and then that’s the image that I feel is happening in a body. You actually become sovereign enough, and brave enough, and self-permitted enough to choose for yourself first, and other people second. That’s the shift.”

I told her that last line made me think of someone I know. She’s smart, she knows what she wants, and she keeps handing the decision back to the good girl. The story about what she should do wins out over her own happiness more often than not. I can watch it from the outside, going in circles.

What It Looks Like at 4 A.M.

Bordo shared an example from earlier that morning. Her best friend’s mother was dying, with perhaps 48 hours left, and Bordo was due to fly out very early the next day. She had been on the road for 12 straight days and had a Reiki appointment booked for 3:30 that afternoon.…

item.title: Know Nothing: Finding Openness in Uncertainty
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear, well-structured English with useful vocabulary

Know Nothing: Finding Openness in Uncertainty

By Leo Babauta

The world is overwhelmed by rapid change, economic stress, wild weather, animosity towards our neighbors, and unprecedented levels of uncertainty.

All of us are feeling it in our own way. It’s a lot to deal with.

In the midst of this uproarious uncertainty, each of us reaches for our protection mechanisms: the ways we’ve learned to gain some sense of control in the uncontrollable.

Those protection mechanisms are familiar:

- We judge others, and turn to blame and lashing out, instead of finding empathy and compassion

- We avoid, hide, procrastinate, and go to distractions and comforts, instead of facing the discomfort of change

- We drive ourselves to work harder and harder, until burnout comes

- We get stuck in perfectionism and indecision, instead of taking action or being vulnerable

- We harden in our opinions and judgments, rather than being curious

- We seek systems of control, optimizing, getting more tools, relying on AI for answers, instead of being open to possibility and discovery

I could go on, but I think you get the idea. We’re thrashing about wildly as we feel out of control.

I’ve found that it’s absolutely possible to find calm and even openness in the midst of this kind of uncertainty. Not easy, but possible.

The answer is in what I like to call the Know Nothing approach. Let’s take a look!

Needing to Know vs. Not Knowing

All of our protection mechanisms (look at the list above) are forms of needing to know, to be in control, … but we’re in a situation where we can’t know, and where we can’t control things.

We want to judge and blame, so we know who’s wrong. We avoid to stay away from the discomfort that we don’t know we can handle. We overwork and optimize and get stuck in perfectionism, trying to control things to turn out the right way. We harden into our opinions, as if we could create certainty this way.

This is all to avoid staying in the space of not knowing. But that’s where we are — we don’t know how things will turn out right now, and we don’t know what to do about that. We simply can’t know.

What if we didn’t need the solid ground of knowing and controlling?

Not knowing is letting go of our demand to be in control and certainty, and opening to the idea that we can survive in the uncertainty … and even find some spaciousness.

We can also discover the delight in the not knowing:

- The ability to be surprised and to discover

- The curiosity to learn when we let go of already knowing

- The thirst to really get to know our fellow human beings, rather than putting them in predetermined categories

- The deliciousness of play, which doesn’t need to be in control

Our deepest learning, love and intimacy, and joy are all possible in this place of not knowing.

How to Live, with the Not Knowing Approach

Living with this approach of not knowing isn’t about being passive or not planning anything. It’s about being open, curious, playful, and open to discovery.

What if we could plan, but hold the plans lightly with an attitude of adventure?

What if we could be in a moment without needing to get anywhere, but instead just be present and savor the experience?

What if we could be with another person, without needing to categorize them first, letting go of any judgments we might have so that we can sit with them and get to know them?

What if we could let down our armor, and be vulnerable?

Each day, we could say, “I don’t know what today may bring. May I be open to it.”

We could walk through the day with a rough agenda, but also be willing to be present with someone in need who isn’t on the agenda, or to explore and play when the opportunity arises.

We could take on our tasks with an attitude of wanting to learn, rather than needing to get through it or get it right.

We could let go of expectations, and be open to finding out.

How to Practice

The main thing is to notice when you’re reaching for your armor. Notice if you’re judging, blaming, avoiding, shutting down, rushing, trying to get it perfect or right.

The best way to notice is to recognize what it feels like in your body: you’ll feel tightness and possibly anxiousness. You’ll feel like you’re bracing against danger.

When you notice that, you can try relaxing your body physically with some breathing and relaxing of your tighter muscles. And then relax yourself mentally as well: into not knowing, softening, opening, curiosity.

You might also have a mantra, like, “I don’t know” or “I know nothing.”

When you say this, drop your story of what you think or how you think it’ll go, or what you know about someone else. And then just see. Be open.

When you’re reaching for answers (like an AI tool, or other tech tools) … there’s nothing wrong with that, but could you take a breath and ask a question instead? And then go for a walk, and let yourself wonder and explore.

I’d like to leave you with a Zen koan (from the Book of Equanimity), which goes, “Not knowing is most intimate.”

In this sense, not knowing isn’t a problem, but the opportunity to be fully present with this moment, without a fixed idea of who we are or who we should be, or what the world should be.

I invite you to practice with this not knowing for the next week, and see what “I don’t know” could yield for you.

item.title: “An Air of Magic”: Scandi, Shaker, and Snug Lodgings in Bovina, New York
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting topic, but less depth and learning value

Have you, like us, pored over the handwritten menus and Shaker-style dining room of Bovina Farm & Fermentory and wanted to book a trip to upstate New York?

“The world of hauling laundry baskets, bed making, sneaking treats onto pillows, and rising with the sun to bake bread for breakfast is one which certainly suits us,” Elizabeth wrote to us a few weeks back. With the addition of a new-build guest cottage, a redone bedroom evocatively called the Pasture Room, and two lodgings above the restaurant, those who come to Bovina for home-brewed beer and a candlelit communal meal can tuck in afterwards in linen sheets and bed down by the heat of a wood stove.

By way of background: “We began building the main house and brewery barn in 2019 with the help of a local barn builder and my father,” Elizabeth writes. “We took about two years to reach ‘completion’—completion in quotes because things are constant works in progress around here.” The two welcomed dinner guests downstairs (read more about the restaurant here) and stayed, meanwhile, in the empty apartment upstairs. “Jake and I lived there for a while with no furniture. I remember sitting on a quilt on the floor with our new puppy and reading through old cookbooks weeks before our opening. We were radiating with anticipation and truly couldn’t care less that we were living in a construction zone.”

Fast forward a few years, and the couple has finally finished the lodgings they envisioned. “We wanted the inn spaces to match the simple, airy interiors of the dining room in the farmhouse, but with some extra warmth and comfort layered in. We stuck with the basic staples you might find in an old farmhouse or tavern: striped bedding, wrought-iron candlesticks, wooden stools that serve as bedside tables. There is minimal art or flourish in our spaces, as we like the views down the valley over the cow pasture or out toward the sheep paddock or into the woods and ferns to do the talking.”

Today, Elizabeth takes us on her rounds about the inn. Join for a tour:

Photography by Sarah Elliott, courtesy of Bovina Farm & Fermentory.

The Cottage

“Jake and I built The Cottage from the ground up, mostly just the two of us, but pulling in many friends and my father along the way,” Elizabeth says. “We built out the foundation in the winter of 2023—it was a particularly mild December and January.

“Even as a build site, The Cottage had an air of magic all around it—it was hard to pull ourselves away up the hill to get back to the restaurant sometimes. Before we started, this plot of land was densely wooded and thick with ferns and brambles that made a nearly impenetrable forest floor. It hadn’t been touched by human hands for maybe 70 years, and the beauty of that was obviously striking. We gently took down trees, leaving as many as we could, and watching this plot of land carefully transform under our nose has been magic all on its own.”

The green interiors were inspired by the land the cottage sits on, “its own secluded patch of woods ” studded with cherry trees. “The exterior, the interior walls, the cabinetry, and the bed nook curtains are all varying shades of green: Farrow and Ball Bone, Farrow and Ball Vert de Terre, DeVol Wikes Green, and a green blue linen gingham, respectively.

“The wood floors and butcher block countertops are cherry. Our neighbors recently restored their old farmhouse using cherry trees that they cut and milled from their own mountain, and we realized how integral cherry was to our area’s original homes and furniture. The depth and warmth of the dark, toasty cherry immediately welcomes you in and makes you feel held in a space. I think cherry is due for a comeback in interior design, but really we chose it simply to match the trees and materials that have been used in our region for hundreds of years. I’d say that’s the trick to nailing interiors: using natural materials that are found in your region. (Take it with a grain of salt coming from someone with no design background.) Like in the restaurant: What grows together goes together.”

“Whenever we’re about to embark on a new build, even for an outbuilding like a new chicken coop or woodshed, we head to The Shaker Village in Hancock,” says Elizabeth.” Every time, we see a new bit of architectural ingenuity or innovation that inspires us and reminds us to stay grounded in design that is beautiful due mostly to its hardworking functionality.”

There are pieces by small makers and friends, too: The pendant above the kitchen table is by “local friend Camille Callahan, who also makes sconce versions, candlesticks, and other objects.”

The Bedroom

The Maison

More details made by artists and friends, according to Elizabeth: “We asked Kelli Cain, local ceramics artist and owner of Luck Dragon arts supply store in the neighboring town of Delhi, to make our coffee mugs for the inn. The hand-dipped beeswax tapers placed around the guesthouse and restaurant come from family-owned Green Tree Home Candle in nearby Treadwell, NY. Maura O’Connor, artist and longtime family friend, drew up the detailed property map that is placed in each inn room and Stephanie Hare of Share Studios in Downeast Maine supplies the handmade papers that Elizabeth scribbles dinner menus on each week. The list goes on—we are so lucky!”

“The sun rises, we slip out of bed and into the arms of a warm oven loaded with dutch ovens filled with baking bread. We work quietly, hoping to wake our guests only with the smells of coffee and rye sourdough wafting their way through the floor vents. The morning gives way to breakfast and farm chores, and then to garden tasks, housekeeping, or whatever jobs are beckoning us that day. Fires are tended to;…
